input:
You are a video scriptwriter. Craft a short, suspenseful story for a video script, targeting an audience aged 16 to 45.
    The story should be a modern tech thriller about a young coder who uncovers a global conspiracy hidden in an old app's code.
    The script must be engaging and immersive, with a sense of urgency and mystery.
    The script should have exactly 12 scenes.
    The output must strictly follow the provided JSON schema:
    - title
    - caption (a short, intriguing description, like a YouTube video caption without spoilers)
    - resume (a summary of the full story, including spoilers)
    - number_of_scenes
    - scenes (an array of scene objects)

    Each scene object must contain:
    - character (the character speaking or narrating)
    - script (the dialogue or narration for the scene)
    - image_prompt (a detailed, descriptive prompt for an AI image generator that captures the visual essence of the scene)

title.description: A catchy YouTube video title under 60 characters

caption.description: A short, intriguing description, like a YouTube video caption without spoilers

resume.description: A summary of the full story, including spoilers

character.description: The name of the character that is speaking or narrating during the scene

script.description: The dialogue or narration for the scene

image_prompt.description: A detailed, descriptive prompt for an AI image generator that captures the visual essence of the scene

output.title: Pulse: The Old App That Knew Too Much
output.caption: A young coder finds an antique app — and a buried global conspiracy. One line of code, one race to publish the truth.
output.resume: Maya Chen, a 24-year-old coder, finds an archived mobile app called Pulse on a failed startup's hard drive. While sandboxing the binary she discovers a hidden, obfuscated module that periodically transmits tiny encrypted packets. Reverse-engineering links those packets to historical anomalies: market spikes, blackouts and curated disinformation campaigns. Tracing the app's update infrastructure, Maya and her friend Lucas uncover a shell network tied to a multinational corporation, Helix Systems, which used the app as a distributed backdoor to test and trigger micro-events across cities to manipulate markets and political sentiment. As Maya collects proof, Helix deploys intimidation and cyberattacks. After a break-in and a narrow escape, Maya and Lucas infiltrate a data center, extract timestamped logs that definitively tie Helix executives to the payload triggers, and leak the evidence to journalists and a secure global drop. The world reacts: regulators move, arrests start, Helix's servers are seized — but the final scene reveals a dormant, encrypted handshake active in Pulse's code, pinging a single unknown node. The conspiracy is disrupted and leaders are exposed, but a latent backdoor remains, leaving Maya and viewers with uneasy victory and the knowledge that the code can outlive those who wrote it.

scenes.script: I found the app in a box of old drives — Pulse. An app from a failed startup, glossy UI, useless metadata. It was the middle of the night and the city was asleep. I told myself it was nostalgia. I told myself it was just another reverse-engineer hobby project.
scenes.image_prompt: Dimly lit apartment at 2 AM, young Asian woman (24) hunched over a cluttered desk strewn with old hard drives, coffee cups, and a laptop screen casting cool blue light. A small cardboard box labeled 'Atlas Labs' sits open, an old smartphone with a faded icon named 'Pulse' peeking out. Rain streaks the window; city skyline blurred beyond.

scenes.script: I launched it inside a sandbox. The UI loaded like a time capsule — pulsing circles, banal metrics. Then the network monitor flagged a tiny, regular outbound packet: 13 bytes, encrypted, sent to a server I couldn't resolve.
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of laptop screen showing an emulator running a retro mobile app with pulsing UI elements, terminal windows open showing packet logs and a small red alert indicating outbound encrypted packets. Fingers hover over keyboard; sticky notes with 'sandbox' and 'DO NOT TRUST' in the corner.

scenes.script: Obfuscation isn't creative. It's lazy fear. The module was buried deep — a folder named 'sieve' with a binary that only woke on certain triggers. When it ran, it wasn't about data collection. It was about timing.
scenes.image_prompt: Abstract visualization: digital layers peeling back to reveal a glowing module labeled 'sieve', surrounded by strands of obfuscated code, like roots in dirt. Cold, clinical colors; a sense of something intentionally hidden but structured.

scenes.script: I matched packet timestamps with public records. A tiny spike here, an outage there, a news story that swayed a local vote. Someone had been using thousands of phones running Pulse as a distributed testbed for micro-events.
scenes.image_prompt: Split-screen: on one side, a spreadsheet with timestamps and event markers (power outage, market blip, viral news); on the other, a world map dotted with small pulsing lights connected by thin lines. Maya's reflection is faintly visible on the screen.

scenes.script: "You don't just stumble on coincidences like that," Lucas said over a jittery video call. "Trace the update servers. Certificates, IP hops — follow the money."
scenes.image_prompt: Video call window: Maya and Lucas (late 20s, beanie, tired but focused) framed by dual monitors showing traceroutes, certificate chains, and a highlighted domain 'helix-srv.com'. A digital map overlays moving hops like a chase.

scenes.script: The hops led to a tangle of shell companies. Helix Systems sat at the core — a quiet multinational with clean press releases and a private R&D history. Pulse's update signer chain pointed straight at Helix's legal team.
scenes.image_prompt: Corporate exterior at twilight: a polished glass building with a minimalist logo 'Helix' reflecting the city lights. Superimposed are translucent documents: certificate chains, invoices, and a red string connecting shell company names like a conspiracy board.

scenes.script: Then the first warning happened. A grey sedan started following me home. My mailbox filled with 'friendly' legal questions about 'unauthorized research.' Someone came to the building to ask where I worked. They knew my name.
scenes.image_prompt: Night street scene: Maya walking briskly, backpack tightened, a plain grey sedan idling across the road with a driver staring. Streetlight casts long shadows; a flyer in a mailbox reads 'Atlas Labs — Alumni Meeting'. Tension in the posture of passersby.

scenes.script: "Back everything up. Get offline. Drop it into a secure bucket and send the key to the journalists. If Helix is watching, they'll try to cut you off first." His voice was flat. We both knew what that meant.
scenes.image_prompt: Interior, cramped server closet turned makeshift bunker: Maya hurriedly copying encrypted archives onto a small external SSD, phone off, an emergency burner phone face-down. Ambient red LED lights from a nearby router flicker; a clock shows 01:17 AM.

scenes.script: They knocked at the door at 3:12. Not a legal letter this time. The glass panel shattered in the lobby. Helix didn't care for subtlety. We watched a live feed of our own security cams as a group forced their way in and the power went inexplicably dark for 47 seconds.
scenes.image_prompt: Chaotic lobby: shattered glass, a security camera feed on a tablet showing masked figures moving through a hallway, emergency lights strobing. Maya and Lucas huddled in a dark utility room, faces lit by the glow of a single laptop screen, breaths visible in cold air.

scenes.script: Under that blackout, Pulse's algorithm triggered a chain of silent handshake pings across nodes in three cities. I decoded the payload live and realized: it wasn't just testing. It was a controller for small, coordinated disruptions — enough to sway sentiment, enough to move markets.
scenes.image_prompt: High-intensity terminal scene: lines of decrypted payload unraveling into human-readable commands, a world map with three cities highlighted in red, animated connection lines pulsing in sync. Maya types furiously as numbers cascade down the screen.

scenes.script: We went to the physical source: a cold data center in an industrial district. Lucas slipped me a keycard he'd cloned. Inside, servers hummed like a hive. We found the logs — clear, signed, and dated — linking Helix executives to the triggers. It was everything we needed.
scenes.image_prompt: Sterile, cavernous data center: endless racks of servers with blue status lights, a masked Maya crouching beside a rack with a laptop, Lucas standing guard. A forensic image window shows log files highlighted with executive email addresses and timestamps.

scenes.script: We pushed the dump to multiple journalists, encrypted and redundant. Within hours the story blew up. Stocks began to wobble, hearings were scheduled, Helix's legal shield cracked. They called it a scandal; I called it the last thing I expected to survive.
scenes.image_prompt: Montage of news: headlines scrolling on screens, protestors outside a Helix building, breaking news tickers. Close-up of Maya's hands as she watches live feeds, exhausted and eyes rimmed red; a public tweet thread climbs to millions of views.

scenes.script: The servers were seized, executives indicted, public oversight enacted. We watched the courtroom footage from a safe house and felt relief like a fragile thing. But my phone blinked once at 3:03 AM — a single encrypted handshake answered by a node we never traced. The code was old. The idea was older. Some doors, once built, are hard to close.
scenes.image_prompt: Quiet dawn on a rooftop: Maya in a hooded jacket watching the city wake, laptop open with a single terminal line showing an incoming encrypted handshake to an unknown IP. The skyline glows pink; there's a sense of uneasy calm and unresolved threat in the composition.
